stories.title_en: Coveting a Fellow Merchant's Fortune Only to Lose One's Own

paragraphs.en: Zhang Pei of Xiuning in Huizhou was a great merchant, with several thousand taels of capital. At Guazhou he bought more than three hundred piculs of cotton. Liu Xing of Shexian was a poor, lonely man. He had long gone out peddling with a shoulder pole and for more than ten years had not been home. By hard saving he had gathered a little over seventy taels of capital, and he too came to this shop to buy cotton. The two were of the same prefecture but different counties. The moment Pei met him, their home dialect matched; he took him for a man of his own native place. They found each other congenial and became as close as brothers. When each had finished buying his cotton, they sold it together at Chen Si’s shop in the Fujian provincial capital, where his lodging was arranged with Pei's as inner and outer quarters.

A few days later, Xing sold all his cotton. Pei had sold only a small portion and collected over five hundred taels. Seeing the silver, Xing conceived a crooked scheme. He conspired with Zhao Tong, a solitary man living next door: "A guest in my shop has a large sum of silver. You hire a boat at Nantai and wait. When I bring it out, we board immediately, then find a mountain temple along the way to hide in, splitting the loot evenly." Zhao Tong agreed. Xing feigned to Pei: 'I intend to go with a fellow townsman to Haicheng to buy southern goods; he hasn't arrived yet, so I must wait a few days.' One day, when a merchant invited Pei to lunch, Xing dug through the hidden compartment in the wall, stole all the five hundred-odd taels from Pei's chest, and packed them into his own luggage. He hired a porter, claiming a townsman had come to urge him to leave quickly. Xing pretended: "My luggage is ready, but Brother Zhang has been invited to drink and cannot say goodbye." Pei's servant replied: "The master isn't back yet; I'll convey your respects." Xing then departed from the host, Chen Si. Chen Si, an experienced broker, looked around Xing's room, but the hole Xing had dug was already concealed by items. The hired porter pretended to head for the seaport, then vanished, turned toward Nantai, and boarded the riverboat heading up to Shuikou.

When Zhang Pei returned, Chen Si said: "Your fellow townsman has already gone. He asked me to convey his respects." Pei opened the room door, saw a knife-cut on the clothes chest, and cursed, "Damn it!" Upon opening it, he found all the silver stolen. He looked around but found no trace. Chen Si entered Xing's room and examined closely, seeing the water gate dug open. He said: "We cannot let this go. There is nothing for it now. You two, master and servant, hire four porters and go straight to Haicheng. I will take an officer and gather seven or eight men, hire a river boat, and head to Shuikou." So Chen Si went upstream looking for a boat. After midday, a boat came downstream. He asked: "All the way down, did you see a river boat carrying two men with three chests of luggage going up—can we still catch them?" The boatman replied: "There were three men and three loads. They went ashore at Shuikou." The hired river boat did not reach Shuikou until nearly evening, and they saw no one coming or going. In a little while, they saw two herd-boys bringing cattle home and asked: "Were there three men ahead with three loads—did you young fellows see them?" The boys said: "Those three went into Shangyuan Gully." They asked: "What villages are in that mountain gully?" The boys said: "None. There is only a temple, called Shangyuan Temple." Chen Si gave five fen of silver and hired one herd-boy as a guide, heading straight to the temple. By then it was nearly the third watch. Chen Si said: "If we call them to open the door, they will surely run. We will split in two: half watch the front door, half the back. At dawn the monks will open; we rush in together, they won't know how to flee, and then we can catch them." Everyone agreed: "That is right."

When the monks opened the door, the crowd rushed in. Startled, the monk asked, "Where have you gentlemen come from?" Chen Si explained the situation and then asked, "What time did those three arrive at the temple?" The monk replied, "They came when it was already dark and stayed in that loft upstairs. They claimed they had encountered trouble and fled here." The monk led them inside; they surged forward and seized the three. They found Pei’s silver packed as one load, while Xing’s own seventy-odd taels were hidden on his person in a small drawstring sack. All the money was recovered. The three knelt and begged for mercy: "We acted wrongly and took his silver. Please return his share, but leave ours with us." The crowd refused to listen, beat them half to death with stones, took all their luggage, and bound the three men back to Chen Si’s shop. Meanwhile, Pei had gone to Haicheng and had not yet returned.

That day, fellow merchants and local people—no fewer than several thousand—came to watch; Xing's shame was completely lost. A few days later, Pei returned and said to Xing: "Because of you thief, I suffered a bitter round trip to Haicheng. Luckily the original silver is still here, so I will not hold it against you. From now on, be a decent man. If I were to act as you did, I would certainly report you to the officials for punishment." Xing said: "You must remember the two words 'fellow townsman.'" Pei replied: "If we speak of fellow townsmen, that is precisely what ruined me! Out of our past friendship, I will not press charges, but get out at once." Xing said: "Please give me back my silver." But Xing's silver had already been taken by the crowd. Pei then told them, "Give it back to him; I will thank you myself." The people said: "If this thief were reported to the officials, he might not even keep his life. You do not press charges, yet he still dares to claim it!" They wanted to beat him again, but Pei persuaded them to stop. He said to Xing: "Your heart was wicked, leading to this outcome; now you have harmed yourself, and you are not worth pitying. However, out of goodwill, I will give you five taels as travel money." Xing was both grateful and in tears; he covered his head and scurried away.

Note: Ah! Sweet rain after a long drought; an old acquaintance in a strange land. A man sojourning away from home, once he meets a fellow townsman, goes about with him morning and evening and soon forms a close bond, like brothers—that is human feeling. Pei and Xing were men of the same prefecture, in the same trade, sharing lodgings at the same shop; that too is how travelers are placed. How could Xing hide a vicious heart, turn the blade on a man under the same roof, and steal for the sake of the money? He secretly boarded a drifting boat, thinking himself clever; he did not know Heaven’s justice is plain. Treachery and theft are not tolerated. In the end he was caught and beaten by the crowd, too late for regret. Seventy taels painfully saved over several decades were lost in a single morning. He schemed for wealth he did not yet have, and lost the profit he already held—how foolish! I am deeply moved, so I write this down as a warning to the treacherous and greedy who have gone mad with lust for gain, and to tell merchants they should be careful, lest they be deceived by a "fellow townsman" who is in fact a thief.

stories.title_en: Pride Brings a Lawsuit That Costs One's Fortune and Life

paragraphs.en: Wei Bangcai was a merchant from Guangdong, the richest man in the province. He was extraordinarily arrogant and always boasted of his vast wealth. When he traveled for business, no one was worth a glance. One day, he bought a hundred piculs of silk in Huzhou to take back to his home province to sell. In Hangzhou, he hired a large boat, and over twenty merchants shared it. Due to wind delays, they stayed in Fuyang County for five or seven days. His servant always rushed to cook first at dawn; whenever he came and went on the boat and found anything slightly unsatisfactory, he would quarrel with the others. The other merchants, having been together as fellow travelers for days and knowing how things stood—and besides, because Bangcai was so high and mighty—yielded to him. The servants also leaned on their master's power and clashed with everyone daily. Bangcai should have restrained his servant and soothed his companions; instead, he sided with his servant and repeatedly spoke insolently: "You pack of low, inferior scum—who among you dares to stand up to me?" He would often speak in terms of thousands of taels. He also said, "I could buy this whole boat's cargo by myself." He said such things several times. Everyone found it unbearable and hated him deeply.

At that time there was Wang Fengqi of Huizhou, from a great clan of prominent officials. He could not stomach Bangcai using wealth and power to crush others, and said: "Worldly power is fleeting, yet you always talk in thousands of taels. In former days, was Shi Chong's wealth any less than yours? And what became of him in the end?" Bangcai, furious that someone dared challenge him, said: "On this boat there are men senior to a humble man like me, and men with greater capital than mine, yet they have not said a word. You dare step forward and oppose me? I will stake all one hundred piculs of silk, worth several thousand taels, against you!" Fengqi cursed him: "You base creature, you truly do not know your place! Time and again you behave outrageously—you really are a little wretch who does not know death is near! I have several thousand taels to match you, and I will see that you never return alive to your native land!" The two wrangled without stopping. Everyone aboard secretly rejoiced to see Wang and Wei locking horns, feeling greatly pleased at heart. Someone who favored Wang urged them each to retire to their cabins.

The next day, Li Hanqing said behind someone's back: "Luckily we have Brother Wang to make a match for him." Cai heard this, cursed Hanqing and then Fengqi with most insolent language; indeed, Cai's words deeply offended everyone. They could not tolerate it and said angrily: "A whole boat of people bullied by one man! We will smear blood and swear an alliance to settle it with him!" Fengqi said: "Help me. Let me stand against him and vent everyone's hatred. He has a hundred piculs of silk. Help me beat him half dead; he will certainly go and file a charge. We will move his silk and hide it elsewhere. Leave half so we can face him in court and destroy his account books. If he sues me, you must not scatter; hold firm and testify. Then we will sell his silk and use it against him. As the saying goes, 'Use his own goods to defeat him.' A brawl is hardly a homicide case." Everyone said: "That is right. We all want revenge. Swear not to leak it." The plot was set. Fengqi then fought Cai several times on the boat; Cai got the worst of it, ran to the county to sue, and the plaint was accepted.

Fengqi had half of Bangcai's silk carried off and hidden, destroying Bangcai's silk-purchase ledgers and tax receipts from every station. His own goods he lodged at broker Zhang Chun's shop. When Bangcai went on board and saw the silk gone, he fought Fengqi hard; he filed a supplementary plaint, charging robbery of fifty piculs of silk, naming a boatful of fellow merchants and the boatman as witnesses. Fengqi smeared pig blood on his head, had two men carry him into the yamen, and filed a countercharge claiming a life-and-death emergency. He then sent a hundred taels to a broker living off official favors—Magistrate Huo's maternal uncle. Bangcai sent a hundred and fifty taels to the county's jinshi, Wei Xian, and nine top scholars. Fengqi also sent two hundred taels to the same men. Wei Xian and the others first went to the magistrate on Wei's behalf; later their urging letters arrived, the language became disjointed, and they were no longer aligned with either party. When the whole set of witnesses was examined, the boatman and others said: "The fighting was real; we did not see silk being moved." The magistrate ruled the claim of fifty piculs of silk was fabricated; it was only a quarrel that led to a suit; both sides were in the wrong. Bangcai would not accept it and appealed to the circuit; the case was assigned to Judge Chen of the prefecture. Both men had connections; the report followed the county's original finding. Bangcai then ran to the grand inspector, the military governor, every circuit office, and even the Nanjing Ministry of Justice. But the petitions merely copied the original text, so all followed the original judgment.

The two men sued each other for about a year, and Bangcai's remaining silk was all spent. He called an elder brother to come help with the lawsuit; the brother brought more than five hundred taels, which were also mostly used up. Bangcai then fell ill at the inn, and his family sent a paternal uncle to come see him. The uncle was an honest, kindly elder; when he asked how the affair had started, he learned that his nephew's arrogant ways had brought this on. The merchants explained the whole matter and proposed an amicable settlement: each side would put up a hundred taels to settle with the officials, and fifty taels would be drawn from that for Bangcai as travel money so he could head home. On his way home, Bangcai thought of all the goods and wealth he had set out with in his trading days, only to return empty-handed now, and he was overcome with bitter resentment. Mocked and scolded by his whole household besides, his pent-up fury only grew worse. Before long a carbuncle broke out on his back, and within a few months he died.

Note: Ah! Bangcai relied on being hugely rich. Think how he treated servants and fellow villagers: cruel, violent, overbearing. Everyone yielded to him, and that bred a savage stubbornness; he had reached the extreme of arrogance and did not know how to turn back. Once he went out to trade, he was a frog in a well, a fool with a narrow eye; he rattled on about money, knew himself and not others, and never checked his tongue. That drove Fengqi and the rest to fury and to lay a plot, use the silk to press charges, and drag him into court. At first he leaned on having much money, thinking he could buy influence and crush people, and supposed Fengqi and the others were toys in the palm of his hand. He did not know that after appeals through county, prefecture, circuit, the offices, and the Ministry of Justice, his capital would all be gone and he still could not win. By then he was a ram with its horns caught in the hedge—stuck, with no way forward or back; gloom made him ill, and regret came too late. If his uncle had not seen the moment to wrap it up and send him home, he would nearly have died of misery abroad and become a ghost in a strange land. “Humility brings benefit; fullness invites loss”—this has been recorded since ancient times. So even if a commoner outdoes you, do not swagger over others on the strength of rank or state. The Sage’s teaching returns to this again and again. Even princes and great men, time after time, have pride purchase their ruin—how much more so ordinary private men! Even in the inner rooms among close kin, arrogance and slackness that go off the path are already wrong—how much more in a place of sojourn! A merchant lodges in a region with few kin, among people from other parts. Keep hardness and softness in balance, stay composed and hold to clarity, and you still fear an unexpected turn—can you then look down on people with pride? So it is said: treat the many with harmony, and all within the four seas are brothers; swell with pride, and even the people in your boat become an enemy state. Merchants should look at this and examine themselves.

stories.title_en: Sedan Bearers Guide a Young Candidate Down a Lonely Path

paragraphs.en: Chao Shicai was from Jianyang. A youth just coming of age, he went to the prefecture for the xiucai selection but failed and returned home. He had three loads of luggage; hiring porters would cost too much, so he left them on a boat and ordered a servant to watch them. He himself traveled by land in a sedan chair; it was only a one-day trip home. When he hired the chair on the road, he opened his silver packet and took out two qian of loose silver to pay them. The two chairmen peeked from the side: they saw a large ingot. Before they had gone thirty li, they carried him onto a lonely mountain path. Young Chao said: "Yesterday I went to the prefecture by boat. Though I am on this land road for the first time today, an official road should be a through-route with traffic; we should not be in this out-of-the-way place." The chairmen said: "This is the way; just ahead lies the main thoroughfare." They went on, still further into mountain tracks. Young Chao understood, and called out: "I know this is not the main road. You only want the silver. I have on me only one ingot of three taels. My family is worth ten thousand taels, and I am an only son, so giving you these three taels is no matter—why turn to harm?" The two chairmen set him down and said: "Then hand it over, and we will spare your life." Young Chao smiled, undid it and gave it to them, saying: "What a fuss over so little—how petty! Now take me back to the main road." The two chairmen paid no heed; once they had the silver they ran off through the hills.

Young Chao found his way back to the main road. He came to a roadside inn and asked if anyone from his county kept a shop there. People pointed it out. He went in and said to the innkeeper: "I am from the Chao family. I hired chairmen who plotted against me and stole my travel silver, leaving me unable to walk the rest of the way. If you know my family, please hire two chairmen to take me home; I will repay their wages generously." The innkeeper replied: "Your family is a great house; everyone has heard your name. How could I not know?" He served Chao a midday meal at once and ordered two chairmen to take him back. Upon returning home, Chao recounted the plot and how that shop had sent him. His family was overjoyed, saying: "Lucky you escaped their deadly trap! What are three taels worth grieving over?" They treated the two chairmen generously and still sent someone specially to thank the inn.

Note: Young Chao did not know this route at first, but as soon as they carried him into the hills, he knew it was not the main road. Seeing that the two meant harm, he paid them off with silver to escape their deadly hands. Otherwise, he might not have kept his life—how could the silver remain? He also knew to find an innkeeper from his own county, hire chairs, and send himself home safely. Though young in years, his resourcefulness far surpassed others. As the verse says: "Books cultivate talent into officialdom; books add wisdom to the gentleman." Had young Chao not read and understood principle, how likely was he to avoid falling into the trap?

stories.title_en: Holding Out for a High Price, He Loses the Profit

paragraphs.en: Yu Dingzhi was from Xihe County in Yunnan. He was greedy at heart and stubborn by nature, rash in pursuing profit. One day he bought gardenias, took them to Sichuan to sell, and received over eighty taels. He then bought danggui and chuanxiong to sell at Zhangshu in Jiangxi; each picul cost him only two taels six qian, freight included. Upon arrival, although danggui and chuanxiong were still scarce, the price had fallen somewhat compared to before. The broker sold the danggui for him at ten taels a picul and the chuanxiong at six taels a picul. Dingzhi angrily blamed the broker: "The other day the price was twelve taels—why cut so much?" The broker replied: "If only two or three piculs had arrived, we could have followed the old price. Now that over twenty piculs have come, if we used the old price, how would that align with market conditions? If you want a higher price, take it to another shop yourself and sell—why get angry?" Dingzhi wrangled with the broker. A fellow merchant standing by, Zhang Chun, advised: "Your goods have already tripled your money; you should watch the moment. If the price falls further, you will regret missing the crossing when there are no boats left." Dingzhi held firm and would not listen.

A few days later, three or four piculs of danggui arrived; the broker sold them at ten taels and they were gone. Chun advised him again: "That merchant already sold at ten taels—why do you not sell?" He still would not listen. Later two more merchants arrived with fifteen piculs; the broker sold them at seven taels, and they too were gone. After a few more days, another ten-odd piculs came, and sold at only four taels. Dingzhi secretly regretted it too late; the other merchants also sighed deeply for him behind his back. Dingzhi sat another month and more; prices fell and the goods grew cheap. He fell out with the broker, so he shipped the lot on to Jianning Prefecture in Fujian, and sold at only three taels seven qian a picul—lower still than the Zhangshu price, and more boat freight wasted besides. Dingzhi cursed his thin luck, that he was not meant to make money. People said it was not thin luck but a proud heart; not bad timing but too much greed. So I write this down as a mirror for those whose thirst for profit is never filled.

Note: Merchants race north and south for profit; who does not wish to buy widely and reap a rich return? Yet when the times allow you to double your profit, you should seize the moment and sell off your stock. Why be insatiably greedy, only to wring your hands after the opportunity is lost—what good does that do? How harmful greed is! People fail to realize that when goods become dirt cheap, they inevitably trend toward high prices; when they become exorbitant, they trend back toward cheapness. There is no extreme that does not turn back. This is the waxing and waning of yin and yang, the turn of fortune in nature's workings—it is always so. How can one go against the times to indulge a greedy heart? That is why gentlemen from of old have treasured contentment over greed.
